_schema: Real aircraft that somebody really built and really weighed, held out from everything the mass model was written against. This file is to Build.mass_parts() what each motor's `validation` block in motors.json is to the thrust fit, and it exists for the same reason: the reference build's 496 g is asserted in six test files, and every one of those assertions checks the model against itself. THE REFERENCE BUILD MAY NEVER APPEAR HERE. It is the calibration point — 496 g, 11.7:1 and 29% hover were hand-verified on paper before any code existed and every mass constant in Build was chosen so that they came out — so an entry naming frame_5in_freestyle + motor_2207_1960kv + prop_5x43x3 would be the test-that-cannot-fail one level up, and tests/test_build_validation.gd rejects it structurally rather than trusting this sentence. If a real published aircraft happens to use that exact combination, that is genuinely interesting and worth writing down in its `notes` — it is still not held-out data. Each entry carries the three core part ids (the pack is deliberately absent, see below), the reported mass, and a `source` naming the page and the line the number was read off, following the citation discipline motors.json already uses: no citation, no entry. WHAT IS REPORTED IS DRY MASS — the aircraft without its battery — and not all-up weight. That is a narrowing, and it is here rather than in a commit message because it changes what the numbers mean. Two reasons. First, the pack would flatter the model: 240 g of battery in a 700 g all-up weight is the one mass nobody has to predict, and carrying it in the denominator halves every error without the model getting anything more right. Second, and decisively, the packs these aircraft are weighed with cannot be entered honestly — a manufacturer publishes a takeoff weight 'with a 1480 mAh battery' and sells no such pack, and internal_r_ohm and c_rating, both physics-bearing in batteries.json, are published by nobody for any pack. BuildValidation assembles every entry on one stand-in pack and subtracts its mass from both sides, where it cancels exactly; a test proves the cancellation against a different pack rather than trusting this paragraph. The same constraint is why HOVER THROTTLE IS NOT VALIDATED and why this file has no field for it: hover throttle depends on the pack's mass, its resting voltage and its internal resistance, so a stand-in pack does not cancel out of it, it replaces the answer. That is a fact about what manufacturers publish, not about the model, and it becomes possible the day an entry can name a pack whose resistance and C-rating are stated by whoever weighed the aircraft. FLIGHT TIME will not appear here at all: Build.FLIGHT_CURRENT_TO_HOVER_RATIO is an admitted guess and the drag term is one fixed area with no moment arm, so a flight-time miss could come from the mass model or from either of those, and a number that cannot say which half is wrong is not evidence about either. WHAT DOES NOT BELONG: colour, price and vendor links, banned by name exactly as they are in data/parts/. Nor does any number the builder estimated rather than measured — a mass read off a spec sheet is data, a mass someone guessed from a similar build is not. A build whose parts are not all in the catalog is SKIPPED and the reason written down; a catalog part invented to make a build fit is worse than having no validation point, because it produces a green line that means nothing. Every part these entries name was added to data/parts/ with its own manufacturer-published specs and its own source string, in the same commit as the entry that needed it.

builds.name: iFlight Nazgul Evoque F5 V2 O4 6S HD
builds.source: iFlight 'Nazgul Evoque F5 V2 O4 6S HD' product page (shop.iflight.com, product 2260), specification block: 'Weight Without Battery: 436±5g'; 'Takeoff Weight: Approx. 695±10g (With 1480mAh Battery)'. Same block gives the parts: XING2 2207 1750KV motors, Nazgul F5 propellers, BLITZ Mini F722 flight controller, BLITZ Mini E55 4-IN-1 2-6S 55A ESC, DJI O4 Air Unit Pro, frame wheelbase 223±2 mm.
builds.notes: The 20x20 boards are chosen from the published stack size (BLITZ Mini F722 + BLITZ Mini E55 are a 20x20 mini stack, and the frame kit is drilled 20x20), not from which choice fits better. What the model's 35 g loose-electronics lump is standing in for on THIS aircraft: a DJI O4 Air Unit Pro and its antennas, a receiver, battery straps, 360-degree TPU, screws and all the wiring.

builds.name: iFlight Nazgul Evoque F5 V3 O4 6S HD
builds.source: iFlight 'Nazgul Evoque F5 V3 O4 6S HD' product page (shop.iflight.com, product 2397), specification block: 'Weight: 492±5g'; 'Takeoff Weight: Approx. 736±5g (With 1480mAh Battery)'. Same block gives the parts: XING2 2207 1750KV motors, Nazgul F5 propellers, Borg Mini F7 flight controller, Borg Mini 60 ESC, DJI O4 Air Unit Pro, frame wheelbase 236 mm (DeadCat default).
builds.notes: Boards chosen the same way as the V2 entry: the Borg Mini pair is a 20x20 stack and the frame kit is drilled 20x20. This aircraft carries the same motors, propellers and air unit as the V2 entry above on a 13 mm longer wheelbase, and iFlight publishes it as 56 g heavier while publishing its frame kit as only 7 g heavier. That gap is a fact about the two spec sheets, and it is deliberately left in rather than reconciled: it is the largest single thing this dataset has to say about how much of a real aircraft the electronics budget is not accounting for.
